#3710. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.

The Avengers haven't even assembled in theaters yet, and the numbers are already getting awkward for DC.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been watching the early numbers for Avengers: Doomsday with some curiosity, especially after all the continued talk of superhero fatigue (honestly, at this point, I have "superhero fatigue talk" fatigue). The Marvel movie doesn't arrive on the 2026 movie schedule until December, but it's already putting up numbers that would make plenty of released films jealous. According to a new report, it's collected $125 million in worldwide advance ticket sales. Compared with how DC's Supergirl performed this summer, things get pretty uncomfortable for the Girl of Steel.

Forbes reported the $125 million figure on Oct. 31, with roughly seven weeks still separating the movie from its Dec. 18 theatrical release. That's a huge amount of money for tickets to a movie that hasn't even opened yet. It's also strikingly close to the $126.5 million Supergirl earned during its entire worldwide theatrical run, according to Box Office Mojo. That's about a difference of about $1.5 million. Yikes.

Now, before anyone declares Marvel the winner of the latest comic-book movie showdown, there's an important distinction. Doomsday's number reflects tickets sold in advance for future screenings, not the final gross of a movie that's finished playing. The $125 million worldwide figure is also a reported estimate, not a total Disney has publicly confirmed. Still, having that many people commit to seats well before opening weekend is encouraging.

This isn't the first time the movie's advance sales have drawn attention. In September, according to The Wrap, Disney Chief Financial Officer Hugh Johnston revealed that Doomsday had already passed $50 million in domestic pre-sales three months before release. The latest worldwide figure covers additional markets, but both milestones show how early the rush began. I've covered the unusually early ticket rollout before, and there were already signs of serious demand when general sales opened in August.

Meanwhile, Supergirl's numbers paint a much rougher picture. Craig Gillespie's film, starring Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El, opened in June and ultimately earned about $72.4 million domestically and $54.1 million internationally. It's a disappointing result for a major new DC release, even if box office numbers don't tell you whether it's worth watching. I know some fans enjoyed it, and they aren't suddenly wrong just because Marvel fans bought a bunch of tickets.

Of course, Doomsday has some advantages that Supergirl never had. Robert Downey Jr. is back in the MCU, this time playing Doctor Doom, and Anthony and Joe Russo are returning to direct an Avengers crossover packed with familiar faces. The combination of returning heroes and the promise of a major multiverse showdown was always going to attract attention. It's also following a massive year for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which gave Marvel another enormous theatrical hit.

There's another interesting wrinkle: Doomsday opens opposite Dune: Part Three on Dec. 18. I've already written about the so-called "Dunesday" clash and the fight for premium screens, and advance demand for both movies suggests moviegoers could have a very busy holiday weekend. Those early tickets don't tell us which film will ultimately have the longer legs.

For now, I wouldn't call $125 million a guaranteed blockbuster, but it's hard not to be impressed. Supergirl spent its whole theatrical run reaching roughly the same number. Doomsday still has more than six weeks left before it opens. That's one heck of a head start.

Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on Dec 18. As for Supergirl, if you haven't had a chance to see it yet, it's streaming with an HBO Max subscription.

#3708. Sir Patrick Stewart, Theater Titan and ‘Star Trek’ Captain, Dies at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart, the beloved actor of stage, screen, and television, died Wednesday following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” according to his representative, Kelly Bush Novak. The performer, best known in this and every other star system as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the USS Enterprise, first appeared in the legendary role in September 1987. After seven seasons of television, four feature films, several video games, and site-specific interactive experiences, he returned to the character in the age of streaming, finally warping to retirement and surrounded by his crew, in January of 2020. He was 79 years old.

Stewart began his long and prosperous life in Yorkshire, England, as the youngest of three boys. His father was a World War II veteran, and, as Stewart discussed, suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnessing violence against his mother as a child, he said, led to Stewart’s later charity work for causes surrounding domestic violence.

He took theater classes in his youth and befriended a slightly older local lad, the actor-mountaineer Brian Blessed. He went on to study at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, a small, competitive conservatory that began with support from Sir Laurence Olivier, and boasts Daniel Day-Lewis, Olivia Colman, Jeremy Irons, Miranda Richardson, and many others as alumni.

In 1966, at age 26, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, one of the most prestigious theater companies in Britain. During his time there, he appeared as the lead in The Life and Death of King John, as Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and as Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, as well as more than 80 other roles, at the RSC’s main home in Stratford-upon-Avon, in London, and on tour. During this part of his career, he also appeared in supporting roles on television. The two most notable were the BBC production of I, Claudius, in which he played Emperor Tiberius’s double-crossing Praetorian guard Sejanus opposite a who’s who of British thespians (Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, Siân Phillips, Bernard Hill, John Rhys-Davies, Stewart’s old chum Brian Blessed, just to name a few), and as the evil mastermind Karla opposite Sir Alec Guinness in the adaptation of John Le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People.

As the 1970s turned to the 1980s, there were some film roles of note, including the part of Leodegrance in John Boorman’s Excalibur and Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s version of Frank Herbert’s Dune. At one moment in the film, he leads a charge into battle clutching a cute li’l pug. (This same character, without the use of domesticated pets, was played by Josh Brolin in the more recent iteration.)

In 1986, with the original Star Trek still drawing good numbers in reruns and on videocassette, and with the feature films starring William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy doing well at the box office, Paramount thought it wise to update the series for television. Franchise creator Gene Roddenberry, who had worked on a “Phase II” Star Trek project in the late 1970s (which led, eventually, to the 1979 film) soon found himself at the drafting board for Star Trek: The Next Generation.

With a bridge crew of several writers and producers from what we now call The Original Series, the new version, set a little less than 100 years down the timeline, differentiated itself in a number of ways. The most notable change was reversing many of the attributes between the Captain and his first officer. Whereas Captain Kirk was a man of action, Captain Jean-Luc Picard was more cerebral, calculating, and cultured, sharing many characteristics with TOS’s half-Vulcan second-in-command, Mr. Spock. (TNG’s Commander Riker, played by Jonathan Frakes, was a bit more rough-and-tumble, and also likelier to woo interplanetary women.)

Patrick Stewart was not Roddenberry’s first choice (Belgian actor Patrick Bauchau, Yaphet Kotto, Roy Thinnes, and Dark Shadows’s Mitch Ryan were also in the mix). But in time, the not-too-well-known Shakespearean won out. When the casting was announced, a reporter suggested to Roddenberry that by the 24th century, in a time of faster-than-light starships, surely humankind would have found a cure for male pattern baldness, no? “No, by the 24th century, no one will care,” Roddenberry retorted, to the delight of bald guys everywhere.

As Stewart has repeated time and again, he took the gig thinking it was a doomed project, as no one would want to watch a retread of a classic. He figured he’d make a few quick bucks, secure some contacts, then head back to his real job on the British stage. He later called the decision to join Starfleet “the most important thing” in his career and his life.

But the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation did not sail out of spacedock without some bumps. (Please don’t rewatch episode four, “Code of Honor,” if you know what’s good for you.) Though wanting to differentiate itself from TOS was the right move, some of the scripts could have used a little more derring-do, and the Picard character comes off at times as a little too cold. This unease was mirrored a bit behind the scenes, where Stewart experienced a little bit of culture clash.

Most of his fellow cast members were Americans who had worked in TV, like Night Court alum Brent Spiner. They were prone to goofing around in between takes, to the point that Stewart actually called a company meeting to scold them. It did not go over too well, but in time, Stewart began to loosen up. (This has now become a favorite thing for the gang to reminisce about during panels at Star Trek conventions, as everyone quickly became, and remained, good pals.)

The chemistry on the USS Enterprise (the Enterprise-D, if we’re getting specific) synched, and the show was a massive hit, making television history as a model for a successful first-run syndication. (If you happened to be a budding sci-fi nerd in central New Jersey that got both New York and Philly stations, it meant you could watch the show twice in the same weekend—not that I would know anything about that.)

From the first episode of TNG in late 1987, through a crossover to Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, and then feature films ending with 2002’s Star Trek: Nemesis, Stewart’s Picard saved the galaxy countless times with class, strength, and poise. Now is not the time to ask, “Who was the best captain?” But one can say, unequivocally, that Picard was the most quotable.

As TNG transitioned from television series to movies, Stewart, with more time on his hands, saw to it that his first role out of the gate would prove his range as an actor. As such, he costarred in the LGBTQ classic Jeffrey, based on Paul Rudnick’s play, as the flamboyant interior decorator Sterling. It may seem like nothing now, but, in 1995, to see a science fiction hero embracing a gay role was a bold move for progressivism.

In the 1990s, between Trek movies, Stewart played Captain Ahab in a USA Network adaptation of Moby Dick, led a one-man show version of A Christmas Carol, and played Prospero in The Tempest for the New York Shakespeare Festival. Then, in 2000, Stewart took on another clutch role in science fiction, Professor Charles Xavier in Bryan Singer’s version of X-Men.

As the schoolmaster/spiritual leader of Marvel’s mutant population, Stewart has played Professor X in eight features, most recently in Sam Raimi’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. It was through the X-Men universe that he and Sir Ian McKellen forged their delightful and public friendship, which led to the two performing in Waiting for Godot together, and McKellen officiating at Stewart’s wedding to jazz singer Sunny Ozell in 2013.

In 2006, Stewart made the first of several returns to the Royal Shakespeare Company to play Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra. His most recent turn on the boards at his old haunt was 2011’s The Merchant of Venice, once again playing Shylock, for director Rupert Goold.

But after a slew of television guest spots (from Frasier to Extras) and lending his voice to various projects including several led by Seth MacFarlane, an album with classical pianist Emanuel Ax, and a profitable Pontiac campaign, he found himself going back to the future. Star Trek: Picard launched in 2020 with a rocky first two seasons before the ship righted itself for a final, triumphant season in 2023, shepherded by Terry Matalas, that reunited Stewart with the cast (and the more than 35-year-old ship) from The Next Generation.

Patrick Stewart was not Captain Jean-Luc Picard, but he brought him to life. Over 178 episodes of TNG (and countless novels and comic books that you can pretend are episodes in your head, not to mention daydreams) the French space explorer with the English accent was a beacon of righteousness and leadership. He accepted input and analysis from anyone in his crew, but felt no obligation to consensus when his mind was made up. He was bookish but also sexy and liked to keep his tunic straight.

As Stewart aged, he increasingly recognized the degree to which Star Trek meant something to millions (and would defend those hardcore fans when needed!) In 2010 he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II. He won a Grammy in 1996 for best spoken word album for children (a recording of Peter and the Wolf) and in 2008 was nominated for a Tony for a production of Macbeth. He was nominated for four Emmys, though none of them for Star Trek.

During the coronavirus pandemic, he initiated a series on social media in which he read a new Shakespeare sonnet each day. We’ll conclude here with the final one.

#3707. 31 Moments That Made The Dragon Age Series Unforgettable

BioWare’s closure last month has put a lot of focus on the Mass Effect series, as the shutdown also coincided with the cancelation of the fifth game in the studio’s sci-fi series. But the company’s fantasy series,Â Dragon Age, also deserves some eulogizing. All fourÂ Dragon Age games are vastly different, spanning different RPG frameworks, fantasy subgenres, and corners of the world of Thedas. Though BioWare left some dangling threads at the end ofÂ Dragon Age: The Veilguard, it also seemed like the studio was focusing on narrative closure, just in case this was the last time anyone in the studio would get to go back to the universe it had created over four games and 15 years. With BioWare gone, let’s look back at some of the best moments from all four games.

Dragon Age: Origins begins with one of six playable opening chapters, the one you play based on the race and class of character you choose, providing a unique background for your character before they head out into the main story.

The Hero of Ferelden can be part of human nobility facing a tragic series of losses, a castless dwarf struggling to make it in the city of Orzamar, or a mage evicted from the magic school theyâve known their entire life, and those starkly different origin points are only half of the options. These origins define how your hero will be viewed in the dozens of hours that follow, and also function as a starting point for how a new player will view the franchise. I started as a Mage when I first played Dragon Age: Origins in 2009, and have always felt like a veteran of the Circle at heart. Future Dragon Age games would implement this concept of different player backgrounds with Inquisition and The Veilguard, but none would do it as thoroughlyâOrigins was the only time I got to see that history play out in real-time.

No character in Origins is as impactful as Morrigan, the enigmatic Witch of the Wilds. The apostate carries a sense of superiority toward the rest of the party, as well as the trials and tribulations of Thedas. When you meet her in the early hours of Origins, you still donât know much about the world, but her commanding presence elevated by Claudia Blackâs excellent voice performance tells you that she is unlike anyone or anything youâve met so far. Morrigan is one of the few characters in Dragon Age who watches nearly every important moment in Thedasâ history unfold, so seeing her here, both enigmatic but still so young and naive, is chilling to look back on.

After youâve picked your background and lived out whatever trauma is associated with it, Dragon Age: Origins puts you at the center of a battle with a darkspawn horde. Your job is to signal for reinforcements to help defeat an army of bloodthirsty monsters, but before the battle starts, the vibes seem off. The golden retriever King Cailain is jazzed about the incoming battle, though his father-in-law Loghain Mac Tir seems less enthusiastic. The tension between the two is tangible, but who are you to get involved in royal family affairs? However, when you signal for reinforcements, Loghain instead commands his forces to retreat, leaving everyone, including you and his own son-in-law, for dead at the hands of the Blight. Most of the preceding origin stories are full of some kind of betrayal. You might think you would get some respite from it at some point, but Origins doubles down, reminding you that you know nothing of this world and the lengths people will go to get what they want.

Origins is not an entirely grimdark fantasy dramaâsome of the best character interactions come from your party members hanging out with your dog companion. Though Mabari dogs are trained to be vicious combatants, your canine companion is a sweetheart. Many interactions between the party and dog give him a hard time for being a mangy mutt, only for him to be revealed as a sensitive soul who just wants to play. Examine your preconceived notions, Origins crew. The sharp fangs mask that the Mabari is actually a good boy.

There are several points in the Dragon Age series in which a party member can turn on you, but none have ever been quite as shocking as when the religious bard Leliana, and otherwise kind-hearted Wynne, turn on you if you taint the Urn of Sacred Ashes. This is a crime against one of the most prominent doctrines in all of Thedas, and bringing two of the most devout members of the party to watch is bound to cause drama, but Origins takes it a step further by having both of your teammates take up arms against you.

It doesnât matter how far youâve progressed through their personal stories, or even if youâre involved in a romance with Leliana; faith trumps all other emotions here, and you will have to strike down your allies. Youâll face plenty more betrayals during the Dragon Age series, but Leliana and Wynneâs heel turn is still one of the most sudden and violent.

Much like killing Leliana, Origins has a few choices whose ramifications were so earth-shattering that BioWare later had to write themselves out of the box theyâd created so they could re-use characters that could be dead. One of those was the option to kill Flemeth, Morriganâs even more enigmatic mother who allegedly wanted to steal her daughterâs body as a vessel to live longer, though the reality is a bit more nuanced than that. When Morrigan finds out about this plan, she begs you to slay the old woman in her hut in the woods. You can choose to do so or strike a deal with her to spare her in exchange for her grimoire of old spells, but choosing to slay her means fighting her in a powerful dragon form. Itâs a tough fight, but doing so leaves you not with a rewarding cutscene and major story revelation, but instead an unsettling and anticlimactic quiet. Youâre left with more mysteries than you had when you arrived, and the unshakable feeling that you might have killed something far beyond your understanding. Flemethâs place in the Dragon Age universe was too significant to be silenced by something as trivial as death, but for a moment, you feel like you have driven a stake through the heart of something you cannot comprehend.

Dragon Age: Originsâ big moment where all your choices culminate is The Landsmeet, a political meeting where you can finally unmask Loghain for all his crimes and essentially set up the country of Fereldenâs future. Your relationships and understandings formed over the past 50+ hours of video game are put to the test, and things can change drastically depending on how the battles of wits and blades pan out. To this day, The Landsmeet is one of BioWareâs most effective showcases of its ability to sew hours of choices into a final consequence. In just one quest you solidify the future for Ferelden in a way that sends most players down the same path, but colors that result so differently that many players, especially those who donât know every secret the game has to offer, will see something that diverges significantly from what the next player might see.

One of the last major choices youâll make in Dragon Age: Origins comes back to Morrigan. The witch has had more than enough reasons to leave the party considering she doesnât really get along with anyone on the team, but she sticks around long enough to give you a final choice: ending the Blight will cost you your lifeâunless you or Alistair undergoes a blood magic ritual that will transfer the Archdemonâs soul into an unborn child. It sounds like a get-out-of-jail-free card, all you have to do is lay with her for one night or convince Alistair to do it. But Morrigan is cagey with her intentions and says that whether you agree or not, she will leave the party after the final battle. This is why sheâs been here this whole time, but does that mean any connection youâve formed with her was all an act? What will become of this child? Is it going to be like any other child or will it be some darkspawn demon that could bring about just as much pain in the world as the archdemon would? Morrigan gives you nothing to go on, but makes her terms clear. Dragon Age: Origins would go on to have three sequels that would wipe away the ambiguity of this decision, but at the time, all you had to go on here was your trust of Morrigan, or lack thereof. Everything youâve ever been told about blood magic and interrupting the natural order of the Blight should tell you to say âno,â but are you willing to risk it to save your own life? Itâs a fascinating choice. Did Dragon Age do right by it? Your mileage may vary.

With Dragon Age II, BioWare started earnestly looking for a way to franchise the series. It had built itself a new cage as the âchoice and consequenceâ studio thanks to the Mass Effect series, and Dragon Age followed suit by importing your Origins save to pepper in cameos and references to your past deeds. That includes whether or not you killed Flemeth, but since BioWare still wanted to use the mysterious witch either way, it had new hero Hawke unwittingly carry her to safety through an enchanted amulet even as she fought for her life against the Hero of Ferelden. Reviving Flemeth is one of the most effective moments in all of Dragon Age in showing how playing as different protagonists in each game could create satisfying meta moments. As she rises from the ashes, you watch the impact of one of your heroâs actions be undermined by the one youâre playing as now. Dragon Age takes place over decades, and a big part of its appeal is watching different stories youâve helped write weave in and out of one another. Itâs a course correction, but one that is still bone-chilling to watch unfold.

The second Dragon Age differs from the first in several ways, from taking place almost entirely in one city to swapping the tactical RPG battle system for more action-oriented combat. But one of the most notable and interesting changes it made was to the approval system, which integrated a Friendship and Rivalry mechanic so you didnât have to kiss a party memberâs ass to progress their relationship storyline. The difference between Friendship and Rivalry is all about how you challenge their preconceived notions. Each party member has a pretty defined view of the world; the radical mage Anders, for instance, is all about freeing magic users from the Circle at any cost, while the elven slave Fenris has an aversion to magic. Uncritically enabling them will give you Friendship points, and going against the grain will net you Rivalry points. This changes the tone of your relationships significantly, and even someone youâre in a romantic relationship with may greet you with a thorny disposition. Watching those connections gradually change is one of the most compelling parts of Dragon Age IIâs writing. Romancing Fenris as a mage while being rivals was one of the most interesting, angsty relationships Iâve ever experienced in a BioWare game. Itâs a shame the studio didnât keep the system around.

Dragon Age II is all about years of civil unrest bubbling to the surface of one city, and between the conflict with the stranded Qunari and the Mage/Templar War, the former is certainly handled with more care than the latter. While early Dragon Age games had multiple crisis points in which party members can leave the party or betray you, one of the most memorable is when one party member makes a decision not to leave, but to return. Isabela is the cause of the Qunariâs extended stay in Kirkwall, and when sheâs given the chance to run off with a tome they have been searching for, she takes it. If youâve not established a solid enough friendship or rivalry with her, she will never return. If you have, she makes a big heroâs entrance just as the Qunari are about to strike down what remains of the city. She attempts to make amends, showing the growth sheâs been trying her damnedest to avoid since arriving in the city. But then the Qunari leader says she still must answer for her crimes. You can give her up and betray her, or you can fight for her instead, and seeing her be big enough to not sell you and the rest of Kirkwall out for once in her life is one of Dragon Age IIâs most memorable companion moments.

Choosing to fight for Isabelaâs freedom results in a somewhat silly but exceptionally satisfying fight. Dragon Age IIâs action-based combat isnât quite as snappy and tight as The Veilguardâs, but it has some spectacle that can keep it interesting in fights that donât just pit you against waves of enemies being thrown at you. The Arishok fight can go a few ways depending on if he respects Hawke or not, but fighting the giant Qunari in a one-on-one duel is still one of the best combat sequences in the game. You may be in for a tough time if you havenât specâd into a class and build that can handle a solo fight, but in any case, taking down the Arishok and being crowned the Champion of Kirkwall is one of the defining moments of Dragon Age II

One bright spot in Dragon Age IIâs extremely uneven final act is the conclusion to Merrillâs story. The elven blood mage has gone against the wishes of everyone around her in a tunnel-visioned need to bring back a part of her clanâs history, even seeking out the help of a demon. Dragon Age II takes place across a decade, with Merrill at odds with her clan leader Marethari all the while, and yet the leader sacrifices herself to âsaveâ Merrill by allowing the demon she had been working with to possess her instead. Merrill can insist this was meddling and you can be supportive of her or not, but the real people she has to answer to are the clanâs remaining members. Depending on whether you advocate for her or throw her under the bus, you may have to fight the entire clan on your way out. Itâs a brutal mess thatâs tied to the character with perhaps the most emotional range of any party member in the franchise. Itâs such a terrifying, saddening web of contradicting feelings and subverted expectations, all leading to a stunning payoff.

I have a lot of issues with the handling of the Mage/Templar War in Dragon Age II. It creates this complicated political and religious conflict around an oppressed group of people and a tyrannical religious organization but insists that both sides are equally bad, actually. Donât even get me started on how you can convince Anders, the radical mage who is the face of this conflict, to kill the mages he tried to save. But the moment in which Anders, worn down by a lifetime of captivity and oppression, blows up the Kirkwall Chantry is one of the few unambiguous statements the game makes in its final hours. The scene itself is dramatic and shocking and kickstarts a war that would (in theory) shake the foundations of Thedas. It requires everyone in your party to make a stand. There will be no more fence-sitting in this fight, and all your relationships will be tested as your team decides whether or not to follow you into battle. Sadly, the reveals that follow undermine any choice you make, but as a spark that ignites a flame, Andersâ act of terrorism is a statement in a game that otherwise seems unwilling to make one.

A lot of the highlights weâve talked about are big story moments or reactions to your decisions, but one of the coolest things Inquisition does happens literally the moment the game starts. The main menu shows rows of mages and templars marching toward a building off in the distance. Despite where we left them in Dragon Age II, these two opposing sides donât seem to be fighting, so perhaps theyâre making their way to peace talks? Could the future of Dragon Age be written not in blood, but in signed treaties? Letâs press ânew gameâ and find o-

I have heard some fans say the moment in which members of the Inquisition start singing âThe Dawn Will Come,â a hymn of the Chantry, to your main character in a moment of religious fervor is cheesy and cringe, to which I say, fuck you, itâs one of the most incredible moments in the game. Inquisitionâs themes can be radically different depending on how you play the Herald of Andraste. This hero has been unwillingly made a religious figure, with hundreds of people expecting you to live as a symbol for a god you might not even believe in. If you take this approach, playing as a non-believer who actively shouts down the claims of the faithful, âThe Dawn Will Comeâ can be an unnerving, haunting reminder of how much unwavering belief can compel groups of people even as you insist on a different, provable truth. If, on the other hand, youâre undecided or playing as a believer, it can read like a beautiful moment of hope and community. Inquisition allows you to define so many shades of who your character is and see them reflected in a world that struggles with your very existence. And sometimes, no matter how hard you kick and scream, you cannot stop the world from believing what it does. Instead, you can just awkwardly stand there while people sing to you and then complain about it later.

With each subsequent game, Dragon Age has gotten better at illustrating the closeness (or lack thereof) of your companions. Banter in the overworld is good, but seeing the crew actually get together is better. The Wicked Grace scene, in which the party gets together to play a card game, is one of BioWareâs best scenes that make use of a gameâs entire core ensemble. Everyoneâs personality gets a chance to shine, whether theyâre playful, stuffy, horny, or just trying to wrangle all these weirdos together. Itâs delightful, succinct, and has stayed in the hearts of many Dragon Age fans.

The Dragon Age series has always been explicitly queer. For all the diaper-shitting about The Veilguardâs queer themes, Inquisition was examining the life and times of a Thedas gay long before Taash learned the term ânon-binary.â Dorian Pavusâ personal quest remains one of the most memorable in all of BioWareâs canon. It drops combat for one incredibly well-acted cutscene between the Tevinter mage and his estranged father, where itâs revealed that, to continue their bloodline and climb his way up the Tevinter political ladder, Dorianâs father planned to use a blood magic equivalent to conversion therapy in order to force his son into an arranged marriage. Iâve spoken to many Dragon Age fans over the years about what decision they made here, as youâre able to help the two reconcile, or to get Dorian out of there. Iâve never once considered telling Dorian to hear his father out. Itâs one of the best examples Iâve seen of a game adapting the queer struggle to a fictional culture. Dorian becomes a radical because he has seen how low even those he loves will go to maintain power in Tevinter, and it all ties into his identity as a gay man. Itâs a stunning scene that tells you so much about Dorian and where he came from, and lets you gently nudge history as you stand beside him.

Blackwall goes under the radar for a lot of players. Heâs quiet, keeps to himself, and is even in a pretty out-of-the-way spot in your base in Skyhold. A lot of people think the Grey Warden warrior is boring, but theyâre wrong; the big reveals you experience in his companion missions are outstanding. Blackwall tells you heâs a Warden but is secretive about the organization which, if you played Origins, may nudge you to think back to your own experience playing as one. You know why theyâre all tight-lipped on the inner machinations of the faction, so you donât question it. But it turns out, heâs actually not a Warden at all, and is instead an imposter on the run for war crimes he committed years ago. Eventually, the guilt eats at him and he turns himself in to save others from answering for his orders with a hangmanâs noose. This man duped you for dozens of hours, and youâre left with the power to decide his fate. Blackwallâs quest can go one of several ways, whether you leave him to rot, pardon him, or send him to the Wardens to let them decide what happens to an imposter. Whatever you choose, Blackwallâs quest leaves an impression as one of BioWareâs most surprising and subversive. Yâall need to quit calling characters you donât even talk to boring. This shit rips.

Even as someone who likes Mass Effect more than Dragon Age, I have a hard time thinking of a singular quest in the sci-fi series that matches up to Inquisitionâs Wicked Eyes and Wicked Hearts. While you will unsheathe your weapons a few times, this mission is all about politics, charming the worst people youâve ever met, and working the crowd. Running around the Winter Palace, meeting the most powerful players in Orlais, and manipulating the politics of an entire country to your whims is more intriguing than anything you do with a sword or staff. Mechanically, the mission is surprisingly elegant as it codifies social status and attention into something that can be measured by a video game, and itâs intriguing learning more about the figureheads you can rally to your cause. There are several outcomes at the end of this mission, and getting what you want might come down to blackmail, reuniting long-lost lovers, or a betrayal of your own. Itâs unlike anything else in the Dragon Age series, and I havenât seen many studios pull off something like it since.

At one point, it seemed as if Flemeth might be the throughline connecting all of Dragon Age. For two games, she was presented as a manipulator, lurking in the shadows and moving the pieces of Thedasâ chess board to her liking. Then all her machinations finally came to a head in Inquisition when she, Morrigan, and perhaps the child the player helped conceive two games prior, all gather in the Fade. Flemeth seemingly has control of the situation, appearing to hold her grandson Kieran hostage and using him as leverage against her daughter who has been on the run since Origins. But as anger gives way to truth-telling and the moment softens, the two find not total reconciliation, but at least an understanding that neither is in danger from the other. It is a series-best performance from Black and Flemeth actor Kate Mulgrew, bringing together three games of choices and history into one incredible confrontation. Iâm still unsure how I feel about the final echoes of this moment in The Veilguard, but Flemeth and her family reuniting and acknowledging the struggle of love and fear for one another that theyâre caught in remains one of the most memorable interactions in all of Dragon Age

I could just throw the entirety of the Trespasser DLC in here and it would be in the running for best âmomentsâ in the series. The final expansion BioWare released for Inquisition in 2015 isnât just an epilogue for the RPG, but is pretty much the true ending. You say goodbye to all the companions with some silly, heartfelt scenes, engage in some politics, and fight some really memorable battles, but the meat of the DLC is in its final 10 minutes. Solas, the elven apostate who abandons your team at the very end, reveals that he is the Dread Wolf, the trickster god who led a rebellion against the rest of the elven pantheon. He plans to tear down the barrier between the real and spirit worlds, which he believes will revitalize the old world of the elves, granting them immortality once more and destroying everyone else in the process. But youâre given two choices that (before The Veilguard, at least) felt incredibly meaningful as a final word for the Inquisitor: Do you think Solas is beyond saving? And is your organization in a state to fight him? Ultimately, neither of those choices mattered in The Veilguard, despite them being imported into the game at the beginning. But back in 2015 it felt like a victory lap, a final declaration by a character you probably wouldnât get to play again.

BioWare has always been held up as a studio that spearheads inclusive design, but The Veilguard takes this one step further by letting you explicitly determine that your protagonist Rook is trans. This isnât just a cosmetic choice like giving them top surgery scars or picking a voice; it can be part of your characterâs backstory that you talk about from time to time with other characters. Few games have been this thorough about letting you define your characterâs identity, and The Veilguard approaches it with a great deal of care.

The Veilguard continues the trend, started with Mass Effect: Andromeda, of BioWare hiding some of a gameâs biggest lore reveals behind an optional collectathon, but this time they are so far-reaching and important that I canât believe some players may never see them. Collecting wolf statues throughout The Veilguard reveals Solasâ regrets. These are murals depicting memories from the elven godâs long life, and essentially write the creation myth of the Dragon Age universe. When I first played The Veilguard, I did these quests pretty late and they started to turn me around on the game entirely. I had mostly considered The Veilguard less a meal than a series of really good sides, but this was when I as a long-time fan felt like I was really eating. Each reveal was juicier and more surprising than the last, bringing connective tissue to a universe that had often felt disparate and disconnected. God, I canât believe theyâre optional.

A lot of The Veilguardâs choices are binary, but most of them are still pretty compelling. The first world-altering choice comes when you must decide which of two cities to save from incoming dragon attacks: Minrathous or Treviso. Thereâs a lot of emotion tied up in this choice, as well as tactical considerations to make. Your Rook might be from Minrathous, but pursuing a relationship with Treviso native Lucanis. You may be trying to develop partnerships with the radical Tevinter group the Shadow Dragons and feel like you should help them defend their city to not burn bridges. Whatever your reasoning and whatever the consequences, you have to choose right then and there. Your teammates are looking to you for an answer, and you realize that a mere few hours of gameplay ago you were just a contractor helping Varric track down Solas. Rookâs arc is all about them confronting the leadership role that has been thrust on them by circumstance and Varricâs expectations. This is the moment it becomes clear that they might not be cut out for the decisions they have to make, but theyâll have to learn to live with those choices one way or another.

The Mourn Watch necromancer Emmrich is The Veilguardâs best marriage of character and faction culture. He is fascinated by death because he has an all-consuming fear of the end. Emmrichâs goal is to become a Lich, an immortal keeper of the dead, willing to watch life begin and end forevermore. But as his personal quests unfold, his assistant Manfred, a reanimated skeleton, is killed in a battle with a rival Lich. Using his powers, he could bring Manfred back, but doing so would disqualify him from achieving the immortality he desires, as it would show an inability to accept death. How can you be immortal and watch everything live and die in an endless cycle if one death of a loved one compels you to defy the natural order? Iâve heard people make cases for allowing Emmrich to become a Lich, but I chose to advise him to bring Manfred back and leave Lichdom behind. The Lich order may believe his inability to leave Manfred behind as a weakness, but I saw it as an asset. Itâs proof that he loves too strongly to spend an eternity watching everyone he cares about disappear over and over again. Still, I see the argument for the other side. No other choice in The Veilguard so succinctly nails the companion-first format BioWare wanted while saying so much about the world in the process.

The Grey Warden headquarters of Weisshaupt has been referenced since the very beginning of Dragon Age, and after all those years hyping it up, our first experience of it is one hell of a followthrough. The Veilguardâs mission at the fortress is an action-packed and narratively rewarding setpiece packed with reveals about the state of the Grey Wardens and demonstrating just how much of a threat the remaining elven gods pose. Meanwhile, the drama it stirs between your team of usually harmonious heroes is a peak moment for the whole series, and holy shit, that boss fight at the end might be the most challenging BioWareâs ever created.

After you see all of Solasâ regrets, you meet a visitor in the Lighthouse: Morrigan. She gives you one last big lore dump, finally putting a bittersweet bow on the tragic story between her and her mother. She also reveals to you that the figure that has been looming over their hit-and-run relationship is Mythal, the elven god of love who once led the pantheon. Mythal is long dead, but her memories have transferred from host to host in the millennia since. Morrigan is the keeper of her memories now, and believes that if even a fraction of the old god were able to release Solas from all his regret, it might be enough to take him off this violent path. Morriganâs epilogue is introspective and melancholy, but as she directs you to one of the last pieces of Mythalâs soul trapped in the fade, all that family drama is given some meaning. The conversation in which you try to convince Mythal to help you is one of the best in The Veilguard. It branches into multiple topics, giving you several footholds to perhaps convince her that your cause is just. Who your Rook is can play into how effective you are in making your case, and if you canât persuade her, you can always fight her for her favor. Whatever route you choose, this is one of those moments in which you can feel Dragon Age history changing with every dialogue option you pick.

Dragon Age: The Veilguardâs final missions are a kind of greatest hits of BioWareâs best tricks. Itâs got everything: unavoidable sacrifice, avoidable losses determined by whether or not you know your team well enough to assign them tasks befitting their talents, and a culmination of all the strategic relationships youâve built with different factions. It might not be as interactive as Mass Effect 2âs Suicide Mission, but as a series of interlocking decisions bringing you to a myriad of mini conclusions, it far exceeds anything the studio has done in the past 20 years. I was nervous and shaking making those choices, and itâs all portrayed with a level of cinematic finesse that goes beyond anything BioWareâs done before.

When The Veilguard reaches its climax, it becomes clear that all the while, youâve been caught in a battle of ideals between Varricâs hope and Solasâ cynicism. Rook has been a pawn (no pun intended) for Solas. The elf has been manipulating them the entire time in hopes of trapping them in the Fade and resuming his plan. Heâs done this by projecting a vision of Varric who hypes Rook up until they can be cut off at the knees, falling into a state of regret so consuming it traps them within the spirit realm. Here, theyâre guided by Varric through the prison until they discover the truth: Varric died at the beginning of the game, and Solas used his image to nudge Rook along the entire game.

The reveal is incredible because you realize BioWare pulled off a Sixth Sense. No one else speaks to Varric the entire game, but heâs placed naturally enough in each scene that you donât really question that no one else responds to him. You realize that youâve been fooled by Solas just as much as Rook has, and when they mourn their mentorâs loss, theyâre effectively a stand-in for you, the Dragon Age fan. But as despondent as they might be, they still have a job to do, and Varric reminds them that theyâve done everything up to this point by themself. They donât need Varricâs guidance. They already have everything they need.

As frustrated as I was with The Veilguardâs decision to leave the Inquisitor behind for a new protagonist, this twist was what made Rook work for me. The whole game essentially emerges from Varric betting on someone to finish the job he couldnât. His belief in Rook is what keeps the game going, even as Solas tries to manipulate it to his own advantage. It may have been sad to watch Varric go from a city dwarf just trying to make it to a victim of Solasâ pride, but his belief in others lives on.

After four games, pretty much everything Dragon Age has ever been leads to one final conversation with Solas. The Veil is coming down, the rest of Thedas will be burned to ash in the aftermath, and the only way to stop it is for the trickster god himself to bind himself to it. No matter what you do, Solas will end up using his immortal life force to keep Thedas and the Fade separate. But the tenor of your decision still matters. You can knock him senseless and forcibly cast the blood magic spell to hold him there, you can trick him so his magic backfires and leave him helpless as you bind him to the Veil, or you can take the third option. Bringing Mythalâs essence out allows her to release him from her service, letting him lay down a lifetime of regret. Itâs the culmination of learning all the secrets left in this world, and once you have all that understanding, it feels like the most appropriate way to cap off a cliffhanger whose resolution weâve been awaiting for ten years.

Given everything thatâs happened to BioWare in the years following The Veilguardâs launch, what sticks out to me most is how much the game leans into finality. Closure is a key pillar of its storytelling, even if there are hints of a sequel we’ll never get. And if this is the note we had to leave it off on, I’m not upset. I hope the folks who were at BioWare at any point during the seriesâ development aren’t either.

#3706. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

Mamdani and others have called out Google's decision to disable search functionality for schools who opt out of its AI tools.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Saying that it believes "schools should have control over AI in their classrooms," Google announced today that it will turn off access to its AI tools for K-12 student accounts. But there's a catch: Along with those AI tools, it will also disable Google search functionality.

In a blog post entitled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, extolled the virtues of AI tools in "productive struggle," which he described as "enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up."

"That's the philosophy behind Guided Learning," Philips wrote. "In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we're now bringing Guided Learning to more products." Those products include Google Search and Google Classroom.

"After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search," Phillips continued. "Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on."

It sounds like Google Search on student accounts can be re-enabled separately, but that also ushers AI back into the equation: Google said in the update that it is "building Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers." In other words, there is no search functionality on these accounts without AI intrusion.

Speaking to the New York Times, Phillips said "search and AI are deeply integrated," and confirmed that schools can't have one without the other: Students at schools that have turned off Google's AI tools "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Fairplay, a non-profit that aims to protect children from "the exploitative and harmful business practices of marketers and Big Tech," was somewhat harsher in its assessment. "Google's attempt to strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire," Fairplay executive director Josh Golin said in a statement. "Schools should use this opportunity not only to turn off AI, but to teach students that 'Google' isn't a verb, but the name of a surveillance and advertising company whose presence in schools has nothing to do with learning and everything to do with developing lifetime brand loyalty.

Former FTC chair Lina Khan, who was right about Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard, also weighed in, accusing Google of "using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI."

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," Khan wrote on X. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, a longstanding critic of oligopolies and corporate greed, said that "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools. No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.  Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.

As NBC noted, research on the impact of AI in education is still quite limited, and some studies purporting to show meaningful benefits have been found to be flawed. That makes the headlong rush into AI integration, championed by massive AI companies and pretty much no one else, so controversial and potentially dangerous. Trying to force AI into classrooms while the technology's impact on mental health is an increasingly serious concern is audacious, and promises of more rigorous safety standards tend to ring hollow anyway: In October, the attorneys general for eight US states accused competing product OpenAI of ignoring its own safety warnings in pursuit of profit.

Google's new policy on AI in schools comes just days after shares in Google parent company Alphabet took a hammering as the company's AI Mode cut deep into its search business and revenue. I've reached out to Google for more information about the new educational policy and will update if I receive a reply.

#3704. Inside Airbnb.org’s Gala With Jimmy Kimmel, Charli xcx, and Brian Chesky

Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.

“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”

Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.

And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

#3703. Indie game website itch.io expands its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' continues to overwhelm Steam and other storefronts

Indie game storefront itch.io has expanded its AI disclosure filters, allowing its users to better separate games made with the controversial technology from those who don't.

This expansion, revealed on its official BlueSky account, includes Itchio's search page which now features a "No AI" box. By ticking this, users can hide any game on the website that features the generative AI disclosure. Games created using generative AI must have this disclosure to be present on the platform, similarly to Steam, although without an option to describe to what extent the tech was used.

This change comes shortly after itch.io also revealed the number of game pages being made on the website each day had doubled in the past two months. And, of course, the number of games downloaded and purchases have not doubled to match this new supply.

itch.io is also facing issues linked to the sheer file size. The storefront has a terms of service policy against AI spam, which it cited shortly after it publicly announced "a couple terabytes of AI slop" had been deleted.

This change comes as the industry as a whole has been clogged with an influx of AI games. Steam Next Fest had a record-breaking number of demo submissions last month. Developers pulled demos in fear of their game being copied, and with Steam saying it's the developer's responsibility to make their games less copyable.

It's an issue that isn't going away any time soon. Even as Claude creator Anthropic has introduced rules preventing unoriginal game clones, alternative AI tools can still be used to create them, and the process of creating games using AI tools will still allow for hastily made, low effort slop. Perhaps filters, like the one itch.io has expanded, is a workable solution to this on-going problem.

FBI may be in its ninth season on the 2026 TV schedule, but the series continues to keep fans on the edge of their seats. Following OA’s undercover storyline, one would think that things are back to normal at 26 Fed. Unfortunately, there may be another shakeup coming. After the end of this week’s episode, I’m worried that another major exit is near.

Throughout the Dick Wolf CBS procedural’s run, there have been a handful of exits. In the last couple of years, FBI has seen three big departures. It seemed like the curse could be done after Juliana Aidén Martinez’s addition at the beginning of Season 8, but alas, another could be coming.

In this week’s episode, “Atonement,” Scola (John Boyd) told the team that Nina (Shantel VanSanten) was offered to run her own task force. It was great news, but Scola didn’t seem too sure about it. He later tells Eva (Aidén Martinez) that the job is in San Diego. While at first he told Nina not to take it, he eventually calls her to say that she should after his conversation with Eva.

Scola was scared about uprooting their life and moving across the country, which is why he told Nina not to take it in the first place. His hesitation is understandable. He’s lived in New York his entire life, their son, Dougie, is getting older, and he has his job. That being said, Nina’s worked hard to get to where she is, and it’s a great promotion for her, which is why Scola came to his senses and told her she should take it. They’ll figure it out.

Whether Boyd is actually leaving FBI remains unknown. VanSanten is set to return to the series on Monday, November 16, but little has been shared about the episode beyond the fact that the team will work alongside Nina to intercept a criminal on the Most Wanted list. Scola and Nina have gone through a lot over the last several seasons, between breakups, makeups, near-deaths, and welcoming their son. While I would absolutely hate to say goodbye to Scola, it would only make sense for him to follow Nina to San Diego so they can stay together and raise their son in the same proximity and not 2,800 miles apart.

Nothing is confirmed, and it’s not even clear if Nina will end up taking the job. It’s likely we’ll get more information during VanSanten’s return on November 16, but fans may have to brace themselves. Boyd has been on FBI since Season 2. It’s hard to imagine the show without him, but at this point, unfortunately, anything is possible. For now, we’ll just have to wait and see. #3701. How To Pitch Stories To Kotaku

We’ve worked with a ton of different freelance writers at Kotaku over the years. Maybe you want to be one of them! Here’s what you need to know before pitching us stories.

The good ones. Especially if you have a unique angle or access to provide our readers with exclusive insights, information, or high-quality writing about something they never knew they wanted to read about before. This includes, but is not limited to, feature stories, opinion pieces, essays, reported scoops, sweeping investigations, and fascinating interviews.

Most of the pitches we get are for reviews and previews. These are also the easiest things to say no to because everyone else will be publishing them. What Kotaku is most interested in when it comes to freelance pitches are original stories that readers won’t be able to find anywhere else because of a unique angle you’ve crafted, insight you’ve unearthed, experience you’ve had, or information you’ve obtained.

This could be an interview with a developer that surfaces a fascinating insight about a game they worked on a decade ago. It could be a bizarre but intriguing drama that played out in a video game Discord community last month. It could be insights from a studio about why a troubled project still hasn’t shipped or a profile of a group of modders attempting something incredible in one of their favorite games.

The best stories inform and entertain. They have characters, conflict, and tension. Some stories have exciting conclusions. Others remain unresolved and are richer because of it. You don’t have to be pitching the next Pulitzer Prize-winning article to be thinking about these types of things.

Send us your idea for what you want to write with a projected word count and timeline for when it would be filed. Suggest a sample headline and explain what makes the story interesting, why we have to have it, and why there’s no version of it that we’ll be able to find online within five minutes of Googling for it. This pitch should be brief, punchy, and as exciting as the final version of the article you’re going to turn in.

Please also share a link to relevant past work and any public profile you maintain. We don’t need to know your entire life’s story or everything you’ve ever written, just one or two strong samples, whether published at a mainstream website or your personal blog, that help demonstrate your ability to execute on the ambitious idea you just pitched us.

Send them to [email protected]. Or you can reach out to individual members of staff. Don’t hesitate to follow up if you don’t get a response right away. And while we can’t guarantee we’ll get back to every pitch, we definitely read them all. We do not accept work produced by AI agents or drafted with the help of them.

Our rates start at $50 for short news posts (300-450 words). Our standard rate for short features (750-1,000 words) is $150. These include light research and some original sourcing (quotes or information revealed for the first time in this story), and often try to show a trend, convey a larger point, or make a broader argument about gaming and the world, although they certainly don’t have to. Sometimes hyper-detailed anecdotes or chains of events within niche communities make for the most interesting reads of all.

We pay up to $300 for more in-depth articles that require multiple interviews, more intensive research, or lots of hands-on time with a game. Rates for everything in-between and beyond are negotiable on a case-by-case basis. If you show up with a leaked build of Half-Life 3 or an exclusive interview with Shigeru Miyamoto, we can talk.

#3700. COD: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ patch has nerfed UAV Towers so you're not immediately visible everywhere you go

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 patches continue, with the latest delivering some big changes to the game's extraction mode DMZ. The latest hotfix introduced a key balance change to one of DMZ's most controversial mechanics: UAV Towers.

UAV Towers, previously guaranteed to spawn in every Point of Interest (POI) in the map, have now had their spawn logic randomised. Infinity Ward also reduced their spawn rate by 40 percent, meaning you're less likely to find them across the various regions of the map. As noted in the patch notes, that change also prevents multiple towers from spawning the same area. The only exception is the Deadtown area, which factors into DMZ Order progression and requires multiple towers.

By taking away the guarantee that each POI will have at least one UAV Tower, the patch removes one of the core tactics PvP-inclined and aggressive players have been relying on since DMZ's launch. It's common for players to spawn in, and immediately run around activating as many UAV Towers as possible to reveal the movement of enemy players, even if they're not interested in directly engaging them.

Indeed, some of the UAV Towers cover extraction areas, so it's easy for players intending to ruin the day of others as they're extracting to set up elaborate traps. Making matters worse, a particular character trait prevents UAV Towers from expiring, allowing the scans to stay up for the entire match.

Infinity Ward has not commented directly on that trait, but the developer confirmed it's being changed so the Sedative Inhaler - which hides you from UAVs - also works with those trait-upgraded towers, though that change won't arrive until sometime in Season 1.

Finally, today's update further makes it easier to stay undetected by boosting the Sedative Inhaler's duration to 120 seconds, double that of the previous 60, which should help while we wait for larger changes to be implemented.
